utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you and thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. And some preliminaries on our part. As you see, I'm not feeling that well today. I will just make an effort to finish the sitting and make it possible for this witness to finish his testimony today. But if I feel much worse than I am now, I think I will have to go. So that's number one. Number two, with regard to your request to have some exhibits examined by handwriting experts and other experts, and my direction -- directive to the Registry to come forward with some kind of protocol that they have used in the past or that they may indicate as appropriate, being the custodian of certain exhibits. I have been told they would be in a much better position to give us the information if they know exactly which documents you are talking about. In other words, if we are talking of exhibits that are already exhibits in this case, then we need to know that. If they are exhibits maybe in another case, we would need to know that. If they are -- if they are documents, the existence of which you know but which have not yet been tendered into evidence by the Prosecution and they are Prosecution documents, then we need to know that. I mean, because the -- as I said before, it's not much the concern of the Registrar as such because these may and will remain as Prosecution documents. But we need to provide with a protocol which will ensure the safe custody of -- and the chain of custody of all these documents. So I am told that if I get this information from you in particular, then they will be in a position to forward their protocol suggestions almost within the day. Another thing is this that they have asked me: Whether any of these documents have already been examined, whether any of these documents have already been examined by the expert appointed by the Prosecution. That's another matter. And whether you would require the originals, and I'm -- I will explain why. Because practically all the documents that we have tendered in the records of this case, in these proceedings, are photocopies of the original. For forensic examination purposes, most of the time at least you require also the original, without which you cannot make really any serious comparison. So please come forward with all this information so that we try and conclude this at the earliest. Any remarks? Because thing you do have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will explain this very briefly. All of these documents are in the possession of the OTP. The originals are in the possession of the OTP, and we shall certainly ask for the originals. Some of these documents have already been examined by an expert of the OTP. Some of these documents have already been admitted into evidence as Prosecution exhibits; some have not. But within a very brief period of time today and tomorrow we can provide precise data about each category of documents and we shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that. Also, I would like you to think along these lines because I did anticipate this of course. Since in this Tribunal we adopt the practice of ex parte expert reports, examinations and reports, and since as you have just hinted some of the documents that you will seek to have examined by your expert have already been examined by -- by the ex parte expert of the Prosecution, we would like you to do some brainstorming amongst yourself particularly and try to tell or give an indication to the Trial Chamber what would you consider to be the situation if at the end of the day the report from your expert on the same documents that have been examined by the expert of the Prosecution are contradictory. Because at that point in time, these being expert reports, you will understand that we are not experts ourselves in this area and we may need to resort to what we do in domestic jurisdictions, that is appoint our own expert. This takes time. I'm not very much concerned about the money that would be needed because it's necessary and the money will have to be found, but it does take time. And I don't want to have the case prolonged unduly because of this, because basically the findings will probably be of utmost importance, absolute importance, for the final submissions that we will have. So please do take this into consideration, think about it, and we will of course postpone the discussion on it pending the result of the investigations that your independent -- your ex parte expert will make. All right? The other thing: I am advised or told by my Legal Officer that the Prosecution wants to address the Trial Chamber following what I said yesterday relating to the Defence motion pursuant to Rule 70. And document that you have received which you passed on to the Trial Chamber yesterday or the day before yesterday. Do you want this to be done in private session, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session now. Any further preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is only the issue of certification of our appeal, and we're worried that it will become moot fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, the decision will be handed down probably later on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have decided and it's -- has to be -- practically it's all drafted except for a paragraph or two. Yes, let's proceed. Let's bring the witness in, please. Have -- what are the arrangements, Ms. Sellers, do you think you will finish with him today or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe I will be able to finish with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the Victims and Witnesses Unit been informed of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, they've been informed by the Prosecution, but I also understand the Defence has likewise informed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness has been informed, too, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no communication with the witness, but I assume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Good morning to you, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two things: You're still testifying in virtue of -- in terms of the solemn declaration that you made when you first started giving evidence, to testify the truth. And secondly, I want to make sure that you have been informed that in all likelihood in spite of all the efforts that we made, it will probably not be possible to finish with your testimony today. Have you been informed of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to assure you that you are one of the few witnesses who -- whom I cannot blame for this extension of time that is needed because you have been answering the questions to the point without much extra information. So, Ms. Vidovic, take your time. I mean, you said you needed five or ten minutes, but if you need more at this point in time, I'm not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Vidovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we talked about a document in which it was stated that you were commended by the command of Srebrenica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will only ask you the following: You said that there was demilitarisation. Tell me, during the demilitarisation what was the role of armed groups or something that may -- might or might not be called the army there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody had any special role to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did most people hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that around Srebrenica itself at the demarcation line there were groups of men holding the lines; that is, between the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Canadian Battalion was stationed there after the arrival of Morillon there. Units were stationed there with their APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Bosnian forces have any positions in that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If they observed someone carrying weapons, they would confiscate the weapons. If they noticed anyone bearing arms for any reason, they had a mandate to confiscate the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation, did some orders arrive from Tuzla about the reorganisation of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that they wanted certain lists to be drawn up, lists of people who had participated in the fighting, who had ever been at one of the lines, people who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Oric's name mentioned in that context in that period after the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the demilitarisation, only later on. First there was the 8th Operational Group, then the 28th Division. This was all there on paper and that's when I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear then that he was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was appointed commander I think first of the 8th Operative Group and then of the 28th Division. That's when I heard this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please show the witness P460. This photograph bears ERN number 0359296.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you take a good look at this photograph. Do you recognise anyone close to you on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person here, the second from the right, is my own brother, Hajrudin Malagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recognise anyone else on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise Naser. This is my cousin, Muharem Mehmedovic, and this is a group of men from Potocari whom I know by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours whether you know anything about when this photograph was taken and who took it. Have you any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken in late February 1993 or early March, because my brother then arrived from Tuzla by helicopter. In September 1992 together with a group of fighters, they took a wounded man, Ekrem Salihovic, who had been wounded in the neck, in the direction of Tuzla. They broke through -- through a corridor. It was a crazy thing to do at that time, through Zepa and Gorazde and over Mount Igman. And when our people took them to Tuzla, the first helicopter to make the flight in Bosnia and Herzegovina was that one and I think they were showing it where to land. It was in the Jadar area, the industrial zone of Srebrenica, and I remember that they brought with them a certain number of uniforms. And my brother even gave me one. He knew the photographer; I think his name was Phillip. He was on good terms with him. So it was late February or early March. That's when he arrived from Tuzla and that's when this photograph could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the end of February or the beginning of March, what year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you in connection with this photographer whom you say is called Phillip, was this a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina or a foreigner? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he was a foreigner who had arrived in the area. This Phillip liked going around with the fighters. He was a courageous man. I know he was a foreigner. I'm not sure but I think he was from Germany. I'm not sure of this, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you whether he knew this Phillip?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you when this man, Phillip, arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Phillip arrived in late February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If someone were to say that this photograph was taken at Christmas, in January 1993, according to what you heard from your brother would this be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would be incorrect because I remember well and it's probably recorded in the air force archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina that this chopper arrived in late February or early March. My cousin, Muharem Mehmedovic is also on this photograph and he was in Tuzla together with my brother. They arrived together. And even this man here, I think Rijad Salihovic, there were more than one man in the group who arrived by helicopter. So it's impossible for this photograph to have been taken before late February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will put just a few brief questions about the fall of Srebrenica, and they are relevant in connection with some of the evidence in this case and the sources of that evidence. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you heard of Mr. Karremans?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of DutchBat which was stationed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that this person on the 10th of July, 1995, a day before the fall of Srebrenica sent some kind of demand to the Muslim leadership in Srebrenica? Have you any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was with a group of fighters holding the line from Zeleni Jadar from where Serb forces were attacking Srebrenica. And we had pushed their lines back from that industrial zone. I remember well, however, that on that day there was fighting. And Mirhat Salihovic told us that he had received information from Ramiz Becirovic that Karremans had said there would be NATO attacks on Serb positions at that line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before you go on you told us a little while ago that your men from Srebrenica did not hold the lines on a regular basis, if I understood you correctly, but that you only went there if you knew there was to be an attack?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The forces of DutchBat then withdrew to Potocari from the area, and there was no one to prevent the Serbs from advancing. So we had to do something to prevent them from walking into Srebrenica. The Dutch forces had withdrawn from their stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that after their withdrawal, Karremans made this demand to the leadership of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell Their Honours what happened after this. Those groups of yours that went there to defend Srebrenica, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were glad when we heard that there would be a NATO bombing of the Serb forces advancing towards Srebrenica. We retreated, we withdrew. And after that the Serbs simply walked in. There was no NATO bombing, as you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this have any effect on the tragedy that later befell the Muslim people of the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a major factor influencing the fall of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people of Srebrenica, do they hold Karremans responsible and the then-government of the Kingdom of the Netherlands for the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the people have instigated a lawsuit against the government of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has allowed the last question to go forward. I just would like to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I allowed it also because there was no objection on your part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, there was no objection because I thought it was going to be tied into relevance in terms of the source. I really at this point do not understand why that question was put forward, not that there might not be factual truth. But I would like to state that for the record and think that that evidence needs to be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's relevant, we will give it importance; if it's not relevant, we will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if it's action -- application that evidence which has been given be stricken, that's obviously more serious than a mere observation. It's our case that the Dutch government and bodies associated with the Dutch have provided evidence in this case and that this relevant background and that in terms of assessing the objectivity and the weight to be given evidence provided from that source because we say there is a motive for providing evidence against our client. And we can develop that in the absence of the witness on some other occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, you can start with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to start straight away or do you need some time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. If you just allow me to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break at 11.30, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. If you just bear with me for a couple seconds. Your Honour, can I please ask the usher just to push the overhead projector backward or forward because we have a line of sight that isn't exactly direct. That's much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is near enough the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be using --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will really have to make an effort to look at any document which is placed on it. Yes, Ms. Sellers. Cross-examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, as Judge Agius has explained before, I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor. And right now the Office of the Prosecution will be putting questions to you concerning the evidence that you've given and also any other evidence that we feel you might be able to provide to the Trial Chamber that's relevant to this case. And I also want to say that it has already been mentioned and you've been commended that your answers so far have been quite brief and to the point. And may I ask you, can we stay within that framework so we might proceed as rapidly but as cautiously as possible. I'd like to start by asking you a few questions concerning your duties as a reserve police officer in the spring of 1992. You've given evidence that as a member of the reserve police office and, in particular as a Muslim in the reserve police offices, you noted there was a schism or a separation between those of Bosnian descent, police officers, and Muslims. You agree that this is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the spring of 1992 when the schism appeared to grow wider, did you along with other Bosnian Muslim reserve police officers, did you discuss the situation, in particular discuss the situation of arms coming into the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed it among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a reserve police officer, my understanding from your testimony is that you were still bound to respond to your command that was in Bratunac until you withdrew from reserve police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so is it correct to assume that your duties included still looking for crime that might have been committed in the area and, in particular, crime that was committed, whether it was by Serbs or by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we received if someone reported, for example, shooting at Kunjerac or Bjelovac and so on, we wrote it down and sent it on to the Bratunac public security station. We commented on these matters among ourselves, wondering why and how this was happening. There were five of us reserve policeman in Voljavica. We chatted about this informally, you understand; when you hear about some news you talk about it. I don't know if you understand me, but we forwarded reports pursuant to our duties to the Bratunac station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. And in those reports, would you put down the name of the person, where the person lived, identifying information such as that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were duty-bound to report everything we had learned because this facilitated a later investigation. But I have to tell you that no investigations were carried out. For what reason? I don't know. But as for the reports, we included all the details, the source of the information, the time, the location, everything that a police report is supposed to contain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as the times the person's father's name or mother's name, possibly their address, their age or their year of birth, would that be the kind of information you would include in your police reports?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to say yes. I understand perfectly well when you're nodding your head, but for the record.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In case we that information, that is. In case we had all the relevant data for the person in question, the mother's name, her maiden name, or the year of birth. If we knew all of that, we would include it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also take down information that you received from an eyewitness or from someone who had heard any incriminating information, would you take down their information and what they had said?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you maybe clarify what you mean by incriminating information?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take the example of someone saw illegal weapons being transported in Voljavica or weapons that could have been deemed to be illegal. And the person came to you as a reserve police officer to report this. Then would you take down the name of the person reporting it and what they had said and what they had observed about the transporting of illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned earlier on that in these reports there was a box for the source of data. There was no arms being brought into Voljavica; it was a Muslim village. So at any rate, whoever reported this sort of information, we would indicate their names in this category of the source of information, the names of the people, their identities, who told us what -- at what time the description of the events, who did he see at what time in what place, and all the other relevant data that might be helpful in the course of an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that just normal, good police work, these procedures that you've described to me now?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, returning to spring of 1992, you've testified about the transport of illegal weapons from Serbia. My question to you is: Did you become aware of the names of people who might have been consistently or, let's say, more frequently trying to buy, sell, or transport illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of our work we often found out the names of people who had been sighted carrying arms. For example, in the vicinity of Voljavica, a place called Pobrdje, the person that the inhabitants of Voljavica reported most often was Goran Ostojic. Quite simply, he had a Russian-made weapon called Dobosar and it used to be a commonly used weapon in the Territorial Defence of the former JNA. And we had reports from the inhabitants as early as mid-1991. He never made any secret of that. He was carrying that weapon, and he would even use it to shoot birds. But his aim was something else, to show that he had this weapon. He never made any secret of it. Goran Ostojic, I do remember him very clearly. And I saw in these documents that he was in a mortar platoon of one of these units around Pobrdje. He was the son of a person called Radomir, if I remember correctly. And that's what we saw quite often in our reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to speak with other Muslim reserve police officers outside of the area of Voljavica during this critical period of time about the transport of weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely, but I did talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it would seem to me that as part of your duties as reserve police officer, that you would become aware of information, principally in Voljavica but at times information outside of Voljavica, that could affect the security and safety of the citizens in Voljavica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it also correct to assume that information concerning the movements of any weapons or any illegal dealing in weapons would have been something that reserve police officers would have had to be interested in as part of their duty?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was indeed of interest to us, of quite considerable interest to us, in fact. But I didn't have that much time. I was normally in Voljavica and I didn't really have time to ask for a reserve police officer from Tegare and ask if he knew about it. We had two police officers on active duty in Voljavica and they covered other areas and what I mean to say is they were on patrol in other areas and we talked to them quite often, and they had more information than we did. There was Mujo Husic who was on the same patrol as I was when we put a stop to the bringing of arms from Serbia to Pobrdje and Herdjec [phoen] Mirsad. So there were police officers on active duty and they covered the entire area of Bratunac. And they had far more information than we did about these matters, and obviously they would report what they knew to us. Why not? They would tell everything what was going on at that time. Of course we were interested. I mean, you must admit that you would have been interested had you been living in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do admit that, yes. Then would you also agree that police officers in the Srebrenica municipality, your colleagues, certainly would have taken an interest, too, in these very same activities of gun-running, or selling weapons illegally, and would have been on the alert for what would have been deemed criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the police force from Srebrenica, I very rarely had any contact with them. But of course their tasks were the same, to follow any movements in as far as the pushing of arms and illegal weapons in particular was concerned. It's a different municipality. They had their own police administration, their own checkpoints, their own reserve officers. And -- I mean, the municipality of Srebrenica is rather large. There are some villages in the direction of Jadra [as interpreted], Osmace, bordering on to Bajina Basta which is in Serbia and the part of Zepa. It's a large area, and of course they had their checkpoints there and their reserve officers as well as police officers on active duty were on patrol there. They might not have had enough actually, enough staff I mean, to cover the entire area, and that was the case in Bratunac as well. Especially after the killing of two Bosniaks in the village of Kravica, tensions mounted so that the police force had to step-up their efforts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I'm correct also in assuming that the police officers certainly at that point in time wouldn't discriminate whether the crime was committed by a Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Serb, or a Bosnian Croat, or a foreign resident of Bosnia. They would be looking for people who had committed criminal acts, irrespective of their ethnicity or their nationality?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We carried out police officers' duties. Our legal obligation was to make no distinction amongst people when it came to their religious affiliations, so we had to put stop to any kind of criminal activity. And I mean -- I don't just mean pushing arms but also transport, theft, burglary. I mean, we were not there to keep Muslims only in check or Serbs only; it was our legal obligation to keep the situation under control with regard to everyone, no matter what their ethnic group was. It's the same in every country, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was legally allowed to buy weapons and arms in Bratunac or Srebrenica municipality during that spring period? Who could legally purchase arms?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one. If they had a special license issued by the police -- well, a special procedure had to be followed. You had to launch an application and then you would be placed under review in order for them to decide whether you'd be issued with that license, and it could be a license for a hunting rifle or a gun or pistol or whatever. And there was a special service, police service. They had to assess whether, for example, you had a criminal record, whether you were a person that could be trusted with a weapon, that is to say for you to purchase and carry that weapon. And once the procedure had been completed, you would get a special form for a specific weapon such as, for example, hunting rifle, and you would go to a special shop and you would get a license for that particular weapon. And it would be registered. So all weapons in the possession of our citizens were accompanied by these special licenses. So this is the procedure I'm explaining to you about. And records were kept at the police, whether it was hunting rifles or maybe guns. But you could buy no other weapons in any shop in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you probably also could not sell any weapons unless you were an authorised person. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably those shops must have had some kind of an agreement with the arms factories such as the Red Flag. Crnava Vastava at Kragljevode in Serbia was the only arms factory on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and I suppose they had an agreement with that particular manufacturer for them to sell their products.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's why the man you arrested coming across the river with his cache of arms, he was illegally receiving the arms and probably the arms had been illegally sold to him. That's the reason you arrested him, right? Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosta Neskovic didn't cross the river; he was waiting on the Bosnian side. Yes, he was waiting for this delivery of arms coming from Serbia. And I don't believe he himself was in fact selling those weapons. At that time they were being systematically armed by someone. It was an SDS activity. Every village, every single one of their villages was being armed. They had already had the experience of war in Croatia and quite a few volunteers from that area had been sent to Croatia. And upon their return in Bosnian they were the main protagonists and the main murderers, in fact. And they had that experience, and that's why they were getting armed and that's why they were preparing themselves for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina because they saw --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just wanted to have you answer my question, that that activity that he was doing was illegal and that's why you arrested him.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you know Mirsad Halilovic's -- of -- before the war?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew quite a few Halilovics. If that's the person you have in mind, the person who worked at the police station in Bratunac, there was somebody called Halilovic there. I don't know if that's him. I did hear of him but I did not know him personally, if that's the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Becir Bogilovic before the war? Becir.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met Becir Bogilovic for the first time on the 2nd of July when he got there with a group of fighters from Srebrenica in order to help us with the attack on Likari. That's the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know Mr. Naser Oric before the war?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naser Oric used to come to Voljavica quite often. That's where his wife comes from, and so his former fiance was from there and he would come to parties there. And we would be bit jealous, I must admit. It wasn't just for anyone to pick a girl from Voljavica, so we were a bit jealous of him. But I did know him before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, his wife's maiden name, I believe, is Avdic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when he came to Voljavica do you know what job or profession he held during that time?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was either still at the police academy or he had already started working in Belgrade, I'm not sure. I do know he was in Belgrade. As to whether he was still at school or whether he was already working, I could not know. I was never actually in touch with him, but I did know of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you do know that he did become a police officer that worked in the municipality of Srebrenica at a later time during this spring of 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. He also got married to someone from Voljavica and his father-in-law and his mother-in-law used to say that their daughter had married a policeman who is working in Belgrade. And they were from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I would like to show you a Prosecution and Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a joint exhibit. It's P564 and it's D690. The English is on Sanction, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you're going to be receiving what is a book that had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been written by a Mr. Besim Ibisevic and I am going to be looking at page 7 in the English and it's page 118, 119 in the B/C/S. If you could look at this document on that page, and there is a line. I believe it's midway through the a paragraph right after you see brackets dot, dot, dot. And it says: "Naser Oric, a policeman at the Srebrenica police station." Do you see that line, sir?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you agree to your knowledge Naser Oric had gone to the police academy and had worked as a police officer, at least in Belgrade. That was your testimony just now. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did work in Belgrade. I don't know exactly until when, but I do know he did it. I don't know in what year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read a portion of this out to you and into the record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's midway down the page and it is a sentence that begins: "The SJB chief." Do you see where I am, Mr. Malagic? It's right after a very -- fairly large writing of the last same "Salihovic, Sado."

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It states: "The SJB chief complained that his employ, policeman Naser, was absent for days and that he did not report to him. Hamed Salilovic (Sado) asked Ibran to decide whose employ Naser was and under whose orders. It was obvious that Naser was using his connection with Ibran to invoice his duties. Naser became less a policeman and more Ibran's private driver. Secret arms deliveries began. Most members of the SDA IO never found out how many weapons there were, what they cost, and where they went. Those who had the money to buy and distribute weapons kept their mouths shut. Rumours began and there were many stories but there was no time to check. Naser was the right hand on the ground of the men who had the monopoly to distribute and sell weapons. In the Drina river valley, Ahmo Tihic was assigned the thankless task of selling weapons. At Osmaci, Imam Aziz Hasanovic sold weapons which arrived from Potocari. There were other people in the field who took over and sold weapons. At meetings of the SDA IO Ibran always defended his protege Naser against accusations that he was irresponsible and lazy. 'Leave him alone, Sado. Naser is more important to me than he is to you! What he is doing is important for the people,' said the SOIO chairman." My question to you is that the selling and trading of those arms was an illegal activity. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct; it was illegal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for a police officer, even for a reserved police officer, he or she should have been aware of what the law was at that time. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Arms trafficking would have been an illegal action for any citizen. But as far as I can see on the basis of this text, Ibran Mustafic is claiming that Naser was very important to him. Everyone in that area knows full well that Ibran never liked Naser and there is a reference to Ahmo Tihic as well. And if you were to show this document to anyone they would tell you that it wasn't relevant. And as to this information with reference to the mention of Hamed Salihovic within the police force, I wouldn't know about that because it is a different police station in Srebrenica. But as far as I know, Ibran Mustafic never liked Naser, neither did Ahmo Tihic. And their joint involvement of this activity is out of the question. I'm 100 percent sure of that because -- I mean, you don't need to believe me. Any other witness, any other person from that area can tell you about it. I'm absolutely certain about it. I don't know how Besim Ibisevic got his hands on this kind of information, but on the basis of what I've read here, I can say it's absolutely incorrect as far as I know. But everyone else would tell you the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you do not know whether this occurred or not because it does say it was kept secret. My question to you, and you answered in the affirmative, is that would be illegal activity. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that anyone involved in illegal arms trafficking, selling arms, whatever, would be acting illegally. But I went on to comment on this that I just can't think where Besim got this information. Does he have any kind of proof?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another issue that I want to raise, that you mentioned Ahmo Tihic, and you would agree, too, that Ahmo Tihic, if he were engaged in this illegal trafficking, that that would be illegal in that time period. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Sellers, I did not say that Ahmo took part in this. All I said was that he didn't like Naser. Don't put words into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I certainly don't want to do that. My question to you is: If Ahmo Tihic did take part in it, in illegal gun-running -- or gun-running of this nature, that that also would be illegal. And your answer is? Yes or no please.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Azir Malagic taken part in it, it would still have been illegal. I suppose I've made myself clear now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you have, Mr. Malagic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that this be taken from the witness, the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I would like to now ask you and tell me yes or no, do you know anyone named Hari Poljak?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know anyone named Husein Alkanovic -- Alikanovic? Or Husin?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last name, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alkanovic. I might be putting the accent on the incorrect syllable. Alikanovic.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Husein Alikanovic, if he was a teacher in the economic school before the war in Srebrenica, then I have heard of him. But I didn't know him personally. I know that Husein Alikanovic was a teacher before the war in the secondary school specialising in economics. He had a master's degree in economics if that's the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge did he ever become part of a military force or a fighter or become a soldier?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness now to see P72.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I would ask you to just look over this document. It's a document dated the 10th of April, 1992. It's entitled "Contract of Sale." I would like to read into the record what it says under Article 1. "On 10th of April, 1992, a contract of sale was signed in Srebrenica between the Srebrenica Territorial Defence. In the capacity of buyer, represented by Naser Oric, Srebrenica Territorial Defence commander and self-employed businessman, Hari Poljak in the capacity of seller, represented by Husein Aljkanovic." [As read] "The contract of sale refers to the following," I'm now in Article 2, "foodstuffs for Srebrenica Territorial Defence, weapons for Srebrenica Territorial Defence, equipment for Srebrenica Territorial Defence, ammunition and shells for Srebrenica Territorial Defence." Article 3 states: "The currency for calculating and paying the goods covered by the contract shall be by DEM," Deutschmarks. And under article 4 it says: "The seller shall sell and buyer shall buy the following goods in quantities at the prices stated below." And under 4B in particular, it says: "Automatic rifles, 800 pieces at 500 Deutschmarks a piece, Zolja hand-held racket launchers, 50 pieces at 200 Deutschmarks a piece, hand-held rocket launchers, 50 pieces at 500 Deutschmarks a piece, and TT pistols 30 pieces at 500 Deutschmarks a piece." And then it says: "Equipment for Srebrenica Territorial defence. Summer camouflage set, 2000 sets at 300 Deutschmarks. High leather boots, bullet-proof vests." Under 4D we have ammunition. "Ammunition and shells for the Srebrenica Territorial Defence, 7.62 ammunition for automatic rifles, millimetres. 1.000 pieces at 34 Deutschmarks. Osa hand-held rocket-launchers, 1.000 pieces." I'm sorry, one million pieces in the prior one. "1.000 pieces at 600 Deutschmarks a piece. 7.62 millimetre pistol ammunition, 27.000 pieces at 0.30 Deutschmarks a piece." Mr. Malagic, my question is solely: With this contract of sale of weapons at that time to Mr. Oric have been considered illegal, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This contract would have been illegal, yes, but this is ridiculous. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not talking about receipt; we are just talking about the contract. And you agree that that would be illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to see the B/C/S version of this document for a while because I only have available the English text. I just want to establish whether it's signed or not and look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I hand you my copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can put it on the ELMO. We can put it on the ELMO. I just want to say the last page, please, or if there are any -- let's see them one by one, one after the other. I just want to make sure if there are any signatures affixed. Go to the next page, please. I need to see it from top to bottom, please. So you have to move -- yes, okay. That's -- move to the second page, please. All right. And let's move to the 3rd page, please. Can the technicians zoom in the part ... All right. And the opposite side. All right. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I state that this is one of the documents that we've had testimony on from the forensic specialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I would rather prefer not to have any comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, I just wanted to, if you were unaware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, we can remove the document. I just have one small follow-up question, and that is: You did not know the relationship between Ibrahim Mustafic and Naser Oric in the spring of 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see Ibrahim Mustafic, but I don't think he was actually staying there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: You didn't know what type of relationship, professional or personal or otherwise, that he had with Naser Oric in the spring of 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibran Mustafic in the spring of 1992 was not in the area. I think he arrived there after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. I don't know how he arrived or why, but he was not in Srebrenica in this period as far as I know. So there could have been no connection between them. Why won't you let me comment on the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever you want to comment on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- The previous document, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Malagic. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness needs the document back, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Let's give him the document back if he requires to see it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, prior to commenting I just want you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just let him comment first, then put your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this contract I have seen huge quantities of food and weapons and boots and equipment. I assume you know what the situation in Srebrenica was, and I'm sure you don't believe this either. I had a single pair of boots from the outbreak of the war until 1995. It says here "2.000 pairs of boots." My father would take the boots and stick some rubber on the soles. And here it speaks of 2.000 pairs of boots, 800 rifles. In Srebrenica maybe there were up to 400 automatic rifles. That's why I asked to comment because I'm a bit shaken by this; it does not correspond to the actual situation there. You all know what the situation in Srebrenica was like then. Enormous quantities of flour are mentioned here, thousands of people died looking for flour, lost their legs because they stepped on land-mines. You would find a man who had stepped on a land-mine and carry him to a village where there was only a medical technician and they would saw his leg off with no anaesthesia. I have seen this happen with my own eyes because we carried those people after they wandered into a minefield, and yet here there is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mention of vast quantities of food. That's why I wanted to mention this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your comment, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can take the document back from him, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's obvious anything in this document didn't arrive in Srebrenica? Mr. Malagic, nothing in this document arrived in Srebrenica; that's what your testimony is now?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had none of these things mentioned here. I don't believe anyone ever bought or sold this. These are enormous amounts of money, and Husein, as far as I know him, he was a teacher. He had a master's degree in economics. I don't believe such a man would have engaged in such activities. He was a teacher. He taught children in school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Malagic. My next thing I want to ask you is that, in terms of Ahmo Tihic, did you know him or did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be moving into a slightly different area and I think maybe we'll just take the break here. But I do have one last question to Mr. Malagic prior to the break because I think he didn't quite answer my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is: If Ibran Mustafic was not in Srebrenica in the spring period, prior to his leaving Srebrenica you did not know what type of relationship, professional, personal, or otherwise, that he had with Naser Oric. Isn't that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can break at this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 30-minute break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, reluctantly. I'm sorry we are again late, but I'm not feeling well. In addition, we tried to discuss a few things further. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There might be some relief as we updated Defence counsel as well that within our trial team we also suffer from disease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope I have not transmitted it to you and that will be in the records if I did. So let's continue, Ms. Sellers. I'm feeling worse than I was this morning and I think my voice indicates that, but I'm gradually falling to pieces and I have a very important commitment this evening which I'm very keen on not missing. But as it looks, it's not going to materialise. Anyway, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I'm going to now ask some questions in a different area, and that's when you left Voljavica. Your testimony was that prior to coming to Srebrenica you went to Poloznik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there you joined with a group of civilians and a group of armed men, including the man who had would become your commander in Likari, Osman. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it differently. We arrived from Voljavica together with Osman. Osman went to Poloznik together with us and all those people. We didn't find him there; we went there together. When we got there we didn't find any armed group there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. So you claim with Osman, and were you with a group of civilians and a group of men who were either fighters or would become fighters for Osman?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived in that area together with the civilians. There were big groups of refugees, as I said, and we decided to create some kind of protection for those refugees because the shelling was beginning and Serbs were beginning to infiltrate the refugees. For example, in Lasovac and they killed quite a lot of people. So in order to protect the people in the area of Ljuljacka we set up a certain kind of defence in front of those refugees, and Osman was there with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "we," are you talking about men? Are you talking about women? Are you talking about men of any particular age or women of any particular age?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about men of a particular age. Osman was the oldest among us. We might have been 41 or 42, and the rest of us were all younger than him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had the other men who were with you, had they served in the JNA for their year of military service or were they also members of either reserve police forces or any other type of structured group prior to this?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Among them there were quite a few who had not had any contact with weapons and who had not served their military service in the former JNA. Some had only just completed secondary school and some hadn't even completed secondary school. I can enumerate at least a dozen of such men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you would allow me to suggest that among those men you were probably one of the ones who were more educated in terms of a military sense, in terms of a police sense or being a member of a uniformed group. Isn't that correct, Mr. Malagic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The group was not uniformed. As I said, I was wearing jeans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me restate that. You might have misunderstood my question. I'm saying that among that group you probably had more experience, having been a member of the JNA, having been a member of the reserve police, more experience in having belonged to, in the past, a group of uniformed men in a structured environment. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had done my military service in 1986 and 1987. It lasted a year. In that group there were also other men who had done their military service. I was not the only one who had had military training. Is that sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very informative. And also you were one of the few, I imagine, or correct me if I'm wrong, who was also a police officer, a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Voljavica there were five reserve police officers and two active-duty police officers working in the Bratunac public security station at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So among the group that we're talking about now that left Voljavica and went down to Poloznik, how many former JNA members or police officers or reserve police officers were in this group?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that group, there were about ten men who had done their military service. Everyone had to do their military service, and in the group there were about ten such men. In the group I was the only policeman. Most policemen were in Hakija Meholjic's group in Srebrenica later on. But in this group I was the only policeman. Although, when we started working as reserve policemen we didn't have any kind of special training. They simply looked at our characteristics from before the war, and, if you didn't have a criminal record, if you had completed secondary school and you were of good character, they would invite you for an interview and evaluate to see whether you were a suitable person in moral and ethical terms to carry out this job. But we didn't have any kind of police training as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the job you certainly learned, as you've already described to the Trial Chamber, investigative skills, information-gathering skills, and you had to carry a weapon as a reserve police officer. If you could just say yes or no for that. Would you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the group is formed in Voljavica, you've gone to Poloznik, and you testified that you were wearing your reserve military officer's jacket but civilian pants. Were there other people in the group that might have had this mixture of clothing?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all you said the group was formed in Voljavica. No, the group was formed when we arrived in Poloznik with the people. I was wearing a police jacket. It was May; we were sleeping outdoors. The jacket was warm and it was cold; that's why I wore it. As for the others, people might have had a sweater or a sheep-skin jacket. We had what we had taken from our homes. We had to sleep outdoors and you have to understand that in May the nights are very cold outside in the woods. And we had to sleep out in the open. Everybody was in civilian clothes. Nobody had any kind of uniform, a JNA uniform, for instance, or any other kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Malagic. My question was maybe just a little bit too obtuse. I just wanted to know: Did anyone else have a mixture of clothing that might have been, let's say, an old TO reserve jacket, maybe someone else wearing part of a military garb, heavier clothing. Just can you say yes or no, in your group did some people have mixtures of clothes, civilian and military, other than you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you also answer as briefly as you've done now: Were there any persons in your group, any of these I would say adult males, young adult males all under 40, were any of them carrying any type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you want yes or no, it's no. Do you want me to explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they carrying rifles or guns or machine-guns or were they carrying knives or things of that nature, weapons in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had maybe a couple of hand-made guns and knives. And using those hand-made guns was a risky business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, would you tell the Trial Chamber how many men were in your group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said this yesterday, but anyway let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you. There were 25 of us, tops, in that group; 25 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this group stayed in Poloznik for how long, if you could tell us? How many days or ...

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in Poloznik until mid-June, almost a month, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were there you've testified you were defending the civilians in the region. So did you organise patrols or manners in which you could defend those civilians, the group?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised the advance posts where two, possibly three people would observe the communication lines in the direction of Bjelovac and Voljevac and Jovanovici where we might have expected an attack to be launched from. So there were two roads that they could have used in order to launch an attack. And from those advance posts we kept them under observation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you established observation posts. Did you also establish any type of walking patrol?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you establish any form of communicating information to other refugee groups or other men that had formed similar patrol groups like yourself?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no flow of information as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then by mid-June your group and the other civilians who had decided to go to Srebrenica. That was your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a group of civilians, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, among the group of civilians were some family members, and I imagine there were other people from Voljavica that you knew who maybe were not family members. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few people who set off with us. Amongst other people there were my parents and the parents of some other members of the group. Voljavica is a large place. There were quite a few inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, had there been inhabitants from Voljavica had already moved to Srebrenica prior to your group and the civilians going to Voljavica in mid-June?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who had family members in some other villages -- well, of course they set off in -- towards those villages earlier on. And, for example, if they had in-laws in villages around Voljavica, they went up there to the village of Gostilj. For example, there were five to six families from our area and they felt -- they had felt before that they were not safe close to the River Drina and there were such situations in a number of other villages, people who had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read some names and would you just tell me briefly, yes or no, do they come from Voljavica. And please bear with me with my pronunciation. Mustafa Delic, son of Hamed. Is that someone you know from Voljavica or that you know comes from Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bajro Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reuf Suhic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suljic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reuf Suljic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hajrudin Suljic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's a son of Daman. Does that make it any clearer?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you spell the surname again, please, because I want to make sure that we -- it's being pronounced well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The family name, sir, or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Suljic, I have S-u-l-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Suljic. Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Hajrudin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mehmed Malagic, son of Ramo?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's an elderly man. I know him. He's an uncle of mine, Mehmed Malagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Suad Muhic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Petko Mujic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Petko is not a Bosniak name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Betko, B-e-t-k-o?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: B-e-t-k-o, possibly, but if it's a P then it's certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not a P, a B. Yes. So Betko Mukic [sic], with B. Do you know that name, sir?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: B-e-t-k-o, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muhamed Cvrk, C-v-r-k, son of Mehmed. His brother --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. Let me try one more time to pronounce the other name. It's R-e-u-f, Reuf Suhic, Suhic, S-u-h-i-c?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suhic, I did say I knew him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of those persons whose names we have mentioned in Srebrenica during the time period that you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did come across them but I don't know what period of time you have in mind, in particular. This Muhamed Crvk for example, who was in our group with Osman, but not the others. But I would come across them in Srebrenica occasionally, and also, when people fled, they were from Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is he related, Mr. Muhamed Cvrk, is he related to Fikret Cvrk?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Fikret Cvrk also from Voljavica to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Fikret Cvrk is from Zalazje which is a neighbouring village in relation to Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the surname of Cvrk fairly well-known in Zalazje?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very widespread in Zalazje, rather more in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Malagic, when you came to Srebrenica your testimony is that you went immediately up to Likari. I'd like to know --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- When you went to Likari did you go with any of your family members, in particularly your mother, your father?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister's husband is from Srebrenica. He married there before the war, and I took my mother and my father to the village of Zabonja right above Srebrenica at my sister's place. I was with my parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it that your testimony is that none of your family members were in Likari with you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of my family, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Likari with the group of young adult men that you've described to us who were in Pleznik [sic] with you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any members of that group take family members, in particular female family members, with them to Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't a single woman in Likari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm correct in assuming that in Likari we had male fighters, not families? It wasn't a refugee population?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just the inhabitants of Likari there. And as to our people, they were not there apart from us, our group, but other inhabitants had fled elsewhere. Because it would have been too risky for them to flee there because it was the front line basically. So you can't have people being there where there was constant shelling and combat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went directly to what was the front line of fighting outpost. Isn't that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found a group of people from Potcaus there and there was some people from Voljavica there as well who had arrived at the village of Gostilj earlier. And we found them there in those burned-down houses. And Likari was held by Serbs from a body in Zalazje and our people had liberated that village and they managed to free four women who had been held prisoner there. And there was a kind of demarcation line which was established between those villages and Likari, and then we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you just remind me: How high up is Likari? You said it was on a plateau. What's the elevation of Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact altitude, but it was at higher altitude than Potocari on one side and Sase on the other side. It was just -- there was just one mountain which was at a higher altitude. I don't know if you are getting my drift. There were houses at the crossroads in the direction of Obadi and Zalazje, and there were other houses lower down. If you can give me a map, I can point it out to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put a map in front of you very soon. I understand how important it is, but I have one other question before that. I would put it to you that as a matter of fact Likari allowed a good view of Srebrenica and of Potocari as well as Sase and the surrounding areas. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain where my error lies?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica was not visible from Likari. Zalazje couldn't be seen either because of a curve on the road and a forest. You could see parts of certain villages. For example, if you were using binoculars you could have used the part of Sase -- you could have seen part of Sase, that is to say the old management building for the mine, but you could not see the actual settlement because Sase is a broader term. It includes Gradina and Kolonija where workers from Sase used to live. Not everything was visible. There were trees, et cetera. Likari is at a higher altitude but not everything was clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then could you tell me briefly, what was the military value of Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Serbs managed to take Likari, they would have been in control of the area across Srebrenica. They could have had Potocari and they would have been able to put artillery there and actually aim at every village in Potocari including the villages of Gostilj and Peciste. And the people from that area would have had to flee even further, and some other villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would have been targeted as well and that's why Likari was of essential importance. And it was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was of central military importance and it was a position that you manned for almost six months during your stay in Srebrenica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 14th of December, 1992, almost six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've testified, too, that there was an old radio in Likari. Could you just tell me extremely briefly, yes or no: Is the fact that the radio was being used on a high elevation point, did that allow you to receive, be able to overhear, more communications?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
