utterances.text: So not only for purposes of defending Potocari or purposes of seeing places such as Sase, Likari was important in order to be able to receive communications, particularly communications from the Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We listened in to their conversations on a daily basis, as they talked to one another from their positions, not on the phone but using their own radio devices. I mean, their military forces used their own military radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the radio. What I'm interested in right now is that you've mentioned Osman group of 25 persons were there. You've also testified that Naser Sabanovic's group came to Likari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found that group at Likari. They arrived there earlier than we did and it wasn't a Naser but a Nasir Sabanovic from the village called Potcaus. When Potcaus was attacked by the Serbs -- well, it was closer for them to get Likari, across the hill called Potcaus and that's how they got there. Another group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one could say you were reinforcements because there was already another group of men who were stationed or positioned on the Likari plateau?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can] say we were reinforcements because they didn't actually ask for anyone to go up there. We decided of our own accord to go to Likari. We had heard that there were some men from Voljavica there. And we thought if we got to Likari we would be able to go down to our villages Voljavica and Zalazje because we had no other way of getting food. We had to go to Voljavica in order to look for food and that's why we decided of our own accord -- I mean, nobody had forced us to go there, up to Likari, I mean. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a slight correction for the transcript. He -- the witness said: "You can't say that we were reinforcements." And it says in the transcript "you can't say." But he went on to explain it. It says "you can say we were reinforcements," whereas in fact the witness said "you can't say we were reinforcements."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. I think it's also obvious, as you said, from the rest of the transcript. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, was there any time period between mid-June 1992, December 1992 when members of your group were not positioned at Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group that I'm referring to was at Likari, I mean this group of Osman's. After Osman's death Zajko Alic took over as leader of that group. We were all at Likari except when we went to visit our families somewhere in Srebrenica or somewhere else, or to simply wash or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, it was a permanent position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to Likari we saw that it was close to Voljavica and that we had to stay there as close to our own village. I mean, we could have left Likari at any time; nobody would have stopped us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I understand that. I'm just saying you were permanently positioned there during the time period you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not positioned there by anyone. We were simply spending time there. Where else could we go to withdraw into Srebrenica and sit and wait to be killed? I mean, we had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can I ask you then the other group with Nasir Sabanovic, were they also there permanently positioned in the manner which you have accepted?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no other place to go except there. Their families had mostly been chased in the direction of Tuzla and Potcaus and sometimes they would spend the night at the village of Gostilj, sometimes they would come to Likari. But they were moving around that area, Gostilj or some other villages where people would offer hospitality. They would go to those houses in order to take a shower, for example. Potcaus was closer than Voljavica and they could not go down there. They tried a number of occasions, I do remember it clearly, and whoever would try to do so would be captured. Whoever tried to get to Potcaus, I mean. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were on this important, essential, both military point -- plateau, were you aware of other front lines or lines of firing - I'm trying to remember your terminology exactly as you had used it - that were in the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there was a lot of shelling and an attack being launched against Bljeceva which is below Potocari between Bratunac and Potocari, the village called Bljeceva. We did know of that line. There was intense shelling there and we also knew of Pirici and Poloznik where we were before we knew that Chetniks were launching attacks there. And that was where most of our people were who had fled, in fact. Because we were interested in that because we had many of our people up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you just explain to me very briefly: How did you know about these other front lines?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to Bljeceva, you could hear it on a daily basis. I mean, if you were in Likari you could hear the shooting from Bljeceva. And as to Pirici and Poloznik, we knew from before, from before we got to Likari because we were there and our people were going to look for food all the time, and that's how we would get the information about people being killed by shells and about those fierce attacks against Pirici and Poloznik. I mean, people were setting off looking for food at the same -- at that time and there was no way of stopping them. They had to look for food in different places. They were here and there and everywhere going, I don't know, looking for food at a distance of 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you referring to the armed men within the different groups or referring to civilians, in terms of people looking for food?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean people looking for food, mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The armed men or the civilians or both?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't simply get a rifle from Likari and go to Srebrenica or somewhere else. The rifle was needed up there because there weren't enough rifles to go around as it was. So you couldn't just pick up a rifle and go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would leave your weapons in Likari to keep as many munitions there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I would like to remind you that you testified that when you were in Likari that you received no support in terms of food or ammunitions from Srebrenica. Is that your testimony or have I misstated it? Logistics support.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got no logistical support from anyone whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you yourself would have to get food, would you tell me, tell the Trial Chamber, did you go into Srebrenica to get food? Was there food in Likari? Or did you go back to Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got our food only and exclusively from Voljavica at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would return to Voljavica from Likari on a frequent basis or on a regular basis in order to search for food. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was Samed Hasanovic also with you in Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Samed or Samid?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Samed.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Do you mean in our group with Osman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I mean among the different fighters who were stationed in Likari.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name does not sound familiar with reference to Likari and I knew everyone because we spent a long time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you that during your five months near Srebrenica, did you have a chance to walk around the town in Srebrenica while you were visiting your family?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself could only go very rarely, perhaps once a week, no more than that and sometimes not even that often, depending on how things stood up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the distance between Likari and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 8 to 10 kilometres, thereabouts. I can't tell you exactly. It would take about an hour, an hour and a half to get there, depending on what part of Srebrenica you were going to. If you wanted to go to the centre of town it was, yeah, maybe 7, 8 kilometres because we couldn't use the regular roads. We had to avoid the shells. We walked through the woods and creeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I would just ask you: In terms of Potocari, what was the distance between Likari and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4 to 5 kilometres, thereabouts. Perhaps I'm not quite precise, but roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were in Srebrenica you would occasionally see the people whose name I tried to pronounce on your visits to Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown document 458, please, Prosecution Exhibit 458. Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 458 is what the Prosecution team refers to as the military police log, for ease of designation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I understand to give the date in the Bosnian version, the date and that will indicate the page, since it's chronologically. I'm looking at the 6th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's page 9 -- no 8 I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And it starts with "Mustafa Delic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell me, Madam Vidovic, when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And has the witness found it? It's an entry on page 8, I take it, page 8 or page 9. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you indicate -- if you put it on the ELMO I can show you exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you would place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think we have to go to 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand it might be page 9 or 10. Page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, page 10, there it is. It's that page over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, where there is a date of 6 December 1992, and then after it, it says: "Mustafa Delic," and then again: "Mustafa" -- do you see where I'm reading from, sir?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to read a bit of this section: "Mustafa Delic, son of Hamid born 19 July 1963 in Voljavica residing in Srebrenica in Ostoja Petrovic's house. utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked about their names at the outset, whether I knew them and whether they were from Voljavica. And I confirmed that, yes.

utterances.text: I would now ask the assistance of the usher again. And I am turning to in the English version page 14. The date is Saturday, the 12th of December, 1992. I will be assisted with the page number on the B/C/S version in a second. 17 I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I want to make sure that the Defence has located the entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I also want to make sure that the witness has the correct page in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you see in the box: "Seniority, 12 December, 1992," it's followed by: "Hajrudin Suljic, son of Dahmo, born 15 May, 1971, in Voljavica, mother Tima" --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. It's Salkic Jusuf born in Osatica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So while on Sanction while the pages were scrolling I think there were others --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's page 18, I understand. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, do you see where I'm reading now request it says: "Hajrudin Suljic, son of Dahmo, born 15 May 1971 in Voljavica, mother Tima, nee Suljic, served in the army as a member of the police guards." Do you recognise that person's name as coming from Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he was born in 1971 and came from Voljavica, I would certainly know him. But -- well, if this person came from Voljavica, I would be sure to know him, Hajrudin Suljic. I would know him if he was from Voljavica. Perhaps he's not from Voljavica. I didn't now any such person in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that he was born there and could have lived elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can he tell you? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You're right. Your Honour, I withdraw the question. It's a hypothetical, as we've had on direct examination. You don't have to answer that question. Let me move on to another question. I'll withdraw that. I would now ask that we go to page 16 in the English version, 14th of December, 1992. And I have the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it can be 16 because 12th of December was 18. So it's 21, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 22 in the B/C/S. And it starts with: "Mehmed Malagic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, is this the person you referred to, I believe, as your uncle?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you would just follow what it says: "Mehmed Malagic, son of Ramo, born in 1937 in Voljavica, residing in Srebrenica." And he talks about: "We brought the grain from a friend from Potocari. Apart from that, we also brought grain from Voljavica."

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that as some of the things that your uncle did while he was in Srebrenica, that getting grain from Voljavica or from friends in Potocari? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that he brought some grain from friends in Potocari and some from Voljavica. He was an elderly man. He often went to get grain like everybody else in order to survive. I don't know what the purpose of this is. He was an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Then you do recognise those events. In you would still bear with me, I'm now on page 21. "On the 20th of December, 1992," and I will tell you that it is page 28 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just an objection to that commentary "you do recognise those events." He's referred to the fact that his uncle went like everybody else in order to survive, to get grain. He hasn't specifically confirmed that he's familiar with these specific events Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referred to in the -- in this document, and so I would object to that characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your comment on that Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that that was a question. Okay, now if he wants me to pose other questions, that's fine. That wasn't a characterisation of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, did your uncle while in Srebrenica go out at times to get grain and seek food?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones, and thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I'm now on page 21 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Malagic, I'm on page 28 of the B/C/S version. And the date is the 20th of December, 1992. I would like to go down this page where it says: "Suad is on the front in Voljavica and Bekto" - with a B - "Muhic, Suad's father has gone to get food." Are those the names that you recognise when I read the list out earlier in your testimony today? Are you able to find where we are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before he answers because I think the Defence is having problems finding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We do beg the Prosecutor when using such voluminous documents to prepare in advance the page numbers in B/C/S. That's what we always do in the case of English. We're always having problems finding these pages. I've just found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it but the date is not the 20th. It's on page 29. Yes, it is the 20th, but it's only on page 29 in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct because previously we were directed to page 28. Yes, let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's in a position to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, do you recognise the names, and that is Bekto Muhic and Suad Muhic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would ask that we turn to the B/C/S on page -- pardon me?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here Suad is on the position in Voljavica, and Bekto Muhic, his father, has gone to get food. This Suad was never at the positions in Voljavica as far as I know, and I know very well. I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Do you know where Suad was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 20th of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: On the 20th of December, 1992, or there around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know because we were in Voljavica then, that group from Likari, all of us. So I wouldn't know where he was. He's a young man. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please now turn to page 39 in the B/C/S. From my indication here it should be near the top of the page, and we're on page 26 of the English -- 39. The date I have is the 29th of December, 1992. Mr. Malagic, under the -- where it says: "29 December, 1992." Then it says Muhamed Cvrk mother's name Ramiza Suljagic residing in Kazani." Do you see where I am, sir?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says: "He was brought to the military police station at the order of the War Presidency for taking a rotary hoe." And then it says: "I brought the rotary hoe before the war from Voljavica to Bojna. The rotary hoe belongs to my cousin, Mehmed Cvrk, and I brought it." Now, do you recognise the names here as the names that you testified about earlier?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to comment on this because this is the date when I was wounded, and that Cvrk Muhamed was also wounded in Voljavica as well as Mirsad Omerovic and another man. The four of us were in Voljavica together and all four of us were wounded together. I can describe the event to you; it's interesting, if you wish. But I know for certain that Muhamed Cvrk was with us in the group together with his brother Jusuf Cvrk whom I mentioned yesterday and he was wounded on that day together with me. A bomb exploded and I was wounded in the face. He was hit in the arm, another man in the back, and Mirsad was wounded in the leg. And this was at the entrance to Voljavica from Pobrdje. He was with me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is his mother's name Ramiz Suljagic? Is this the man whose mother's name is stated there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I knew his mother but not her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I would like to ask you now -- and you testified earlier that that is the name Cvrk and Suljagic and that family name is known in Zalazje, if I remember correctly, Cvrk?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More in Voljavica than in Zalazje. In Zalazje there were perhaps just two families; there were more in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would now ask you to go back to what is page 8 in the English version. It's the first entry that we looked at. I believe it's page 9 in the B/C/S version, and it's the 6th of December, 1992. And page 9 in the B/C/S version, and it's the 6th of December, 1992. And of course that is the segment that starts with Mustafa Delic, son of Hamid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 10 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it goes over to page 10. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, I would just ask you -- I've read this into the record. Would you look over this entry briefly. We have the names and then it says: "At around 1500 hours Fahro Smajovic fired his TT 7.62 millimetre pistol twice at the door and a VP patrol which came afterwards found one cartridge." And then it says: "At around 1700 hours, the men left and I was alone." It goes on to say: "Just before 1830 hours, when Ahmet Omanovic was wounded, I heard shots from an automatic weapon ..." My question to you, Mr. Malagic: As a former police officer, is this standard manner in which to write down information in a police log?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had forms. If we didn't have any forms, we could enter a description of events in our own words and at the bottom state the source of the information. Let me just have a look here. As far as I can see, there is a description of the event. But there's no information on the people who made statements. You always had to enter the names of witnesses, who was an eyewitness, who was there, their details, the date, the hour, exactly when something happened. This doesn't look like a police report in the real sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is this report containing the information that you testified about earlier in terms of people's names, dates of their birth, their parents, information concerning the reason that they might have been brought in or questioned by a police officer?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people mentioned here, I said I knew Mustafa Delic, son of Hamid. He was from Voljavica. I saw him occasionally but rarely when I went to Srebrenica. Then you see Reuf Suljic from Voljavica, I knew him, too. Omerovic Bajro from Voljavica, I knew him as well. All these are men that I knew from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, now I'd ask you to go to page 4, and it would be B/C/S page 5. It's dated 4 December, 1992. Now, I'm looking at the part that says: "At around 1720 hours, Mirsada Hodzic, residing in Vidikovac, came to the military police station with her common-law husband, Hasib Jusupovic to report Alija Suljic and his brothers for allegedly attacking her and threatening her husband by putting a pistol to his neck while other men beat him." Do you see where I'm reading? Sir, do you see where I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then it continues on to say: "I sent a VP patrol from the station to bring in Alija Suljic and his brother Hajrudin. "The patrol brought the two Suljic brothers at 1920 hours." Is this -- my question: Is this more in keeping with police reporting in your experience as a reserve police officer, the manner in which this entry has been made?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not the manner in which an experienced policeman would draw up such a report. I don't see a signature here. A policeman has to sign the report if he has taken a statement, and this is all in one and the same handwriting in this log, as you call it. It's all in the same handwriting. It's impossible for one policeman, a single policeman, to have written all of these reports. I don't know of the existence of any military police in this period in Srebrenica. The 4th of December. That is when Rifat Suljic [phoen] from Voljavica died of starvation. Had there been a military police at the time, or rather -- I don't exclude the possibility that there was, but I can't say there was. I would find it very odd. But you can see for yourself, it's all in the same handwriting. So it would all have had to be done by the same policeman carrying out onsite investigations. That's impossible. I'm not a forensic expert, but you can see it's all in one and the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, then would you agree that under the circumstances that you've described Srebrenica, that this type of military log would be in keeping with the conditions of a city that was being -- clearly at war?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the entire log, but my uncle is mentioned here. I don't know what he did wrong. He was an honest man. He went to look for food and was brought in by the military police. And about these other events, I cannot exclude the possibility that this police existed. But under the conditions prevailing in Srebrenica at the time, for somebody to have kept this log entering all these dates in all this nice handwriting, that I do exclude as a possibility. This was in December when everybody knew that a Serb offensive was in the offing. And all people could think about is how to survive, whether they could somehow break through. That's what was on people's minds at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's one matter which may be important later. I think we all heard in English the intonation when the witness read: "He went in to look for food and was brought in by the military police," it was as a question. It's an extraordinary statement. In the transcript it comes out as a statement. It's a small point, but I wouldn't want it just to be thought later that he was stating that fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how we heard it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, you're giving a hypothetical proposition that there might have been a military police but you didn't know about it. Isn't that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did not know of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I hope that clarifies it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You can remove the document from Mr. Malagic, please. Your Honour, do you want to continue or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we can stop here -- how much more --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will take at least one or one and a half sessions of tomorrow, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the position with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, I do -- I do want to register a concern about the next witness, quite honestly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I take it there will be a re-examination on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I imagine there will be. I can't see my colleague, but I'm sure there will be. The concern about the next witness is, obviously, he's in The Hague being proofed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's a doctor with an extremely busy schedule and that's something we didn't anticipate, that he would have to stay over the weekend. He might have to come back on a subsequent occasion to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Yes. At least be -- I want to rest your mind, put your mind at rest that we will do whatever's required, saving -- just keeping my fingers crossed that I would be able to make it tomorrow. There's a Scottish remedy that usually works with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and there will be a doctor in the house tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, if we can stop here I think it will be better. Let me go home and try to recover my energies as much as possible so that I will be here tomorrow. Otherwise, if I start getting feverish, I will not come over for sure. All right? Thank you. One moment. I want to explain to the witness. Please sit down and put your earphones back, please. Mr. Malagic, we are stopping here and we will continue tomorrow. We'll definitely finish with you tomorrow. In the meantime you will be escorted like you were yesterday, and make sure you don't communicate with anyone. Thank you.
